papers list --format ris and --format csl-json write the entries to the standard output instead, without copying files (see Output formats). papers add refs.ris and papers add refs.json read these formats (see Add RIS and CSL-JSON files).

docs.title: How the fields are converted
docs.text:
The values are written as unicode (LaTeX accents and commands are converted, braces removed). Fields without an equivalent in the format are left out.

bibtex CSL-JSON RIS key id, citation-key ID entry type type (below) TY (below) author, editor author, editor (family, given, non-dropping-particle, suffix; a name in braces is a literal) AU, ED (Family, Given, Suffix) title title TI journal, booktitle container-title T2 series collection-title T3 year, month issued (date-parts) PY, DA volume volume VL number, issue issue (articles), else number IS pages page (11-29) SP, EP doi, url DOI, URL DO, UR isbn, issn ISBN, ISSN SN publisher (or school, institution) publisher PB address publisher-place CY abstract, keywords, note abstract, keyword, note AB, KW, N1 edition, language edition, language ET, LA file custom.file (a list) L1 (one line per file)

CSL-JSON has no field for files: the links are written in its custom object, "custom": {"file": [...]}, which other programs ignore.

bibtex CSL-JSON RIS article article-journal JOUR book book BOOK inbook, incollection chapter CHAP inproceedings, conference paper-conference CPAPER proceedings book CONF phdthesis, mastersthesis thesis THES techreport report RPRT misc document GEN online webpage ELEC dataset, software dataset, software DATA, COMP unpublished manuscript UNPB

docs.title: Files
docs.text: An entry links to its files (the PDF, supplementary material...) in its file field. The files usually live in the files directory of the library (the filesdir setting), named after the name template (see Renaming files and keys), but an entry can link to a file anywhere.

docs.title: What add does with a file
docs.text:
The files setting says what papers add does with the PDF it adds, with the files of the entries of an added bibtex (papers add other.bib), with the files of an added folder (papers add --recursive DIR) and with the files attached with --attach:

files the file is placed in the files directory the original is removed move (default) yes, under its template name yes copy yes, as a hard link when possible (same file system), otherwise a copy no link no: the entry links to the file where it is no

Set it for a library with papers config files copy, or for all libraries of the user with papers config --global files copy. The options --move, --copy and --link of papers add override it for one command; -r/--rename is the same as --move, and -c the same as --copy.

A file that belongs to another library, i.e. a file inside the files directory of a library whose configuration (.papers/config.json) is found in the file's directory or above, is never moved: in move mode it is copied instead (a hard link when possible), so that the other library keeps its link. The same holds for a file in the files directory of the pool of the library, or of the library of --pool PATH (see Pools). A file already in the files directory of the current library is renamed in copy mode too, rather than copied next to itself. A file downloaded by papers (a URL given to add or --attach) is always moved into the files directory.

In a shallow library (a library with a pool), the file links are the pool entry's; the library decides which entries it has. The files directory where add, file attach and file rename place the files is that of the pool, and the name template is the pool's: move and copy place the file in the pool's files directory, and the library entry and the pool entry link to it there; with link, the file stays where it is, and both link to it there. This works on one machine; on another machine that uses the pool, such links are broken (see Shallow libraries).

docs.title: papers file
docs.text:
The commands of papers file act on the files of the entries. Those that take entries accept keys, DOIs, arXiv identifiers or ISBNs (see Naming entries), and - to read them from the standard input, one per line:

Command Action papers file rename [KEY...] place the files of the entries (all without KEY) in the files directory, under their template name; --keep-source keeps the originals too (hard links when possible) papers file mv SRC... DEST move files or folders, and update the links of the entries (below) papers file attach KEY FILE... attach files to an existing entry, following the files setting (--move, --copy, --link override it); the files the entry already has are not touched papers file detach FILE... [--key KEY...] remove the links to the files from every entry that links to them (only from the entries of --key with --key); the files are kept (below) papers file detach --key KEY... remove all the links of the entries papers file detach --broken [--key KEY...] remove the broken links (of all entries without --key) papers file rm FILE... [-r] [--key KEY...] remove the links to the files, then delete the files, like git rm (below) papers file check [KEY...] report broken links and the files found for them (in the pool, in the libraries of --pool PATH, and in the folders of --search DIR), files linked twice, identical files (same checksum) of an entry, and with --metadata a DOI of the PDF that differs from the DOI of the entry (this parses the PDFs) papers file fix [KEY...] apply the repairs that papers file check reports (below); --pool PATH and --search DIR as for check; the files found are copied, never moved (--move moves those of --search) papers file clean remove the files of the files directory and its subfolders that no entry links to, asking for each one (-y/--yes does not ask)

papers file attach KEY FILE... is the low-level form of papers add FILE --doi DOI for an entry already in the library: when the DOI is that of a library entry, add attaches the file to it in the same way, without fetching anything (see Adding entries).

papers file check changes nothing, and ends with the number of links that papers file fix can repair. papers file fix only applies the repairs that cannot lose anything: paths saved by Mendeley (missing leading /, latex symbols such as {\_}) are repaired when the repaired path exists, the second link to the same file, or to an identical file, is removed from the entry (the file itself stays on disk; papers file clean removes it), and broken links are relinked to the files found for them (see Reconnecting PDFs and a bibtex). The other broken links are reported, and removed with papers file detach --broken.

papers file clean skips hidden files and folders (such as .git) and .bib files. A folder of the layout of versions before 2.19 (with a hidden .<name>.bib) is removed as a whole when no entry links to its files.

docs.title: Moving files
docs.text:
papers file mv works like mv, with the rules of git mv, and updates the links of every entry that links to a moved file (links are compared by real path, so a link through a symbolic link is found too):

  1. a source file that no entry links to is an error;
  2. a source folder must contain at least one linked file; the whole folder moves, files that no entry links to included;
  3. with several sources, the destination must be an existing folder;
  4. a destination that exists as a file is an error, unless -f/--force (papers warns when entries link to the replaced file: their links then lead to the moved file);
  5. -n/--dry-run shows the moves and the links that change, and does nothing;
  6. moving the files directory of the library (or a folder that contains it) also updates the filesdir setting.

All checks run before anything moves: if one fails, nothing is moved. If a move fails midway (e.g. disk full), the bibtex is saved with the links of the files already moved, and the error is reported. The parent folders of the destination are created when needed. A folder that contains the bibtex or the library configuration cannot be moved with papers file mv.

papers file mv files/2013 files/archive/2013
papers file mv files ~/Documents/library-files    # also sets filesdir
papers file mv -n files/a.pdf files/b.pdf files/new/

Links from other libraries to the moved files break: papers cannot know about them.

docs.title: Detaching and removing files
docs.text:
A file can be linked from several entries: the chapters of a book that share the PDF of the volume, two papers that share a supplement. papers file detach FILE... removes the links to FILE from all of them and prints which entries lost a link. Links are compared by real path, so a broken link can be named too. The files stay on disk: papers file detach never deletes a file.

papers file rm FILE... works like git rm: it removes the links to FILE from every entry that links to it, then deletes the file.

  • A FILE that no entry links to is an error, and nothing changes (with --key: that none of the entries of --key links to).
  • -r FOLDER removes the linked files inside FOLDER (and its subfolders). Files that no entry links to stay where they are; the folders left empty are removed, FOLDER included, except the files directory of the library. Without -r, a folder is an error. papers file detach -r FOLDER removes the links in the same way, without deleting anything.
  • With --key, only the links of those entries are removed; a file that another entry still links to is kept on disk, and papers says so.
  • In a shallow library, the link is removed from the pool entry too, and the file (in the pool's files directory or elsewhere) is deleted unless another entry of the pool or of the library still links to it.
  • papers does not ask: the file was named on the command line. --dry-run shows the links that would be removed and the files and folders that would be deleted.

-k/--key takes one or more entries (keys, DOIs, arXiv identifiers or ISBNs), and can be repeated: --key K1 K2 is --key K1 --key K2; - reads them from the standard input. As it takes several values, write the files before it: in papers file rm --key K1 file.pdf, file.pdf would be read as an entry, and papers stops with the error file.pdf is not an entry: put the files before --key.

papers file detach files/volume.pdf                    # from all the chapters
papers file detach files/volume.pdf --key smith2020    # from one chapter
papers file detach --key smith2020                     # all its links
papers file rm files/old-version.pdf
papers file rm -r files/2013 --dry-run
papers list --tag draft --detach-broken

docs.title: Reconnecting PDFs and a bibtex
docs.text:
When the links of a library are broken because the PDFs moved (another library that shared the files directory moved them into a library, a folder was renamed, a backup was restored elsewhere...), papers file fix looks for each missing file, without parsing any PDF:

  1. in the pool of the library, among the files of the pool entry of the same paper (same DOI, arXiv identifier, ISBN, or same title and authors): the file with the same file name as the broken link; else the one file named <name>--<file name of the link> (the pool renamed it as an attachment, see Renaming files and keys); then, if one broken link of the entry and one file of the pool entry are left, that file. When more are left, nothing is guessed;
  2. in the libraries given with --pool PATH (the option can be repeated), in the same way: the entry of PATH of the same paper, and its files. PATH must be a library (otherwise: create it first with papers init). Nothing changes in PATH, and no origin copy is recorded (see Origin copies): only the file links of the library change;
  3. in the folders given with --search DIR (searched recursively; the option can be repeated): a file with the same file name as the broken link, else a file named as the library's name template names the entry (with the extension of the link). When several files match, none is taken, and papers says which.

The file found replaces the broken link. It is never moved, whatever the files setting:

  • in a self-contained library, it is copied (a hard link when possible) into the files directory, named as papers file attach KEY FILE names it;
  • in a shallow library, a file of its pool is linked where it is; a file of --pool PATH or of a --search folder is copied into the files directory of the pool, and the pool entry links to it (as for the other changes of file links, see Shallow libraries);
  • in link mode, or in a library without files directory, the file is linked where it is.

papers file fix --move moves the files found in the --search folders instead of copying them. A file in the files directory of another library is still copied (... belongs to the library in ...: copied, not moved), and so are the files of the pool and of --pool PATH.

papers config pool PATH links the library to the copies in PATH of the files that exist, and says how many links were already broken: papers file fix relinks them afterwards.

papers file check takes --pool PATH and --search DIR too, reports the files that papers file fix would relink and where they come from, and ends with the papers file fix command to run, with the same -C DIR, --bibtex FILE, KEYs, --pool and --search. papers file fix --dry-run shows the links that it would change, and changes nothing. After papers file fix, the last line counts the issues left, if any.

$ papers file check --pool ~/P --search ~/Downloads
perrette2013scaling: broken link: ~/old/esd-4-11-2013.pdf -> ~/P/files/perrette_2013_a-scaling-approach.pdf (from the library ~/P)
perrette2011: broken link: ~/old/bg-8-515-2011.pdf -> ~/Downloads/bg-8-515-2011.pdf (found in ~/Downloads)
2 links can be relinked, 0 without a file found
2 issue(s) in the files of 2 entries
2 links can be repaired: `papers file fix --pool ~/P --search ~/Downloads`
$ papers file fix --pool ~/P --search ~/Downloads
perrette2013scaling: relinked to ~/thesis/files/perrette_2013_a-scaling-approach-to-project-regional-sea-level-rise.pdf (from the library ~/P)
perrette2011: relinked to ~/thesis/files/perrette_2011_near-ubiquity-of-ice-edge-blooms-in-the-arctic.pdf (found in ~/Downloads)
2 links relinked, 0 still broken

papers file fix works on any bibtex, without papers init: there is no files directory, and the files found are linked where they are.

$ papers file fix --bibtex refs.bib --search ~/Downloads
perrette2011: relinked to ~/Downloads/bg-8-515-2011.pdf (found in ~/Downloads)
1 link relinked, 0 still broken

For PDFs whose names say nothing about the paper, papers add -R DIR is the fallback: it parses each PDF, and a PDF with the DOI of a library entry is attached to that entry, without new entry and without duplicate dialogue (a PDF with the content of a file of the entry is not attached again; see Adding entries). The broken links stay next to the new ones: remove them with papers file detach --broken.

docs.title: Removing entries and their files
docs.text:
papers rm KEY... (or papers list ... --delete) removes entries. Their files that no remaining entry links to may be deleted too:

  • in a terminal, papers lists those that are inside the files directory and asks once whether to delete them (default: no);
  • --delete-files deletes them without asking, and also those outside the files directory; --keep-files keeps them without asking;
  • without a terminal (e.g. the keys come from a pipe), the files are kept, and papers lists them: papers file clean deletes them later;
  • a file outside the files directory is deleted only with --delete-files.

A file still linked from another entry is never deleted, nor a file in the files directory of the pool of the library, nor, in a shallow library, a file that an entry of the pool links to (see Shallow libraries); papers rm does not change the pool. In a shallow library, --delete-files is an error and nothing is removed: the files are the pool's, and papers file rm FILE deletes them. A file that is a hard link (e.g. to the file of another library) can be deleted: this only removes this link, and papers says so.

docs.title: Deprecated forms
docs.text: papers filecheck still works in v3, with a warning, and runs the corresponding commands: --rename (-c) is papers file rename (--keep-source), --delete-broken is papers file detach --broken, --hash-check and --fix-mendeley are papers file fix, --metadata-check is papers file check --metadata, and --clean-filesdir (--force) is papers file clean (--yes). papers list --copy and --add-files are deprecated too (now --rename --keep-source and --attach, see Listing and searching), and so is papers add --attachment (now --attach; -a FILE attaches the file until v4, with a warning: -a is --author, see Adding entries).

docs.title: Git integration
docs.text: papers can keep the history of a library in a git repository of its own, the backup directory. Every command that writes the bibtex then commits a snapshot there. This history is what papers undo, papers redo and papers restore use (see Undo and redo).

docs.title: Turning the backup on and off
docs.text:
papers init turns the backup on when the git program is installed (unless the global configuration sets git, see Global configuration). --git and --no-git choose explicitly, and --git-lfs also backs up the attached files (see git-lfs):

$> papers init --bibtex papers.bib --filesdir files [ --no-git | --git-lfs ]
created the library ~/projects/sealevel
* bibtex:  papers.bib
* files:   files (the files directory of the library)
* backup:  git and git-lfs
`papers status -v` shows all settings

The * backup: line says git, git and git-lfs, or off. With --git or --git-lfs, papers init stops with an error before creating the library when git (or git-lfs) is not installed; so does papers config git true.

The setting can be changed at any time:

papers config git true        # start the backup (first snapshot: the current bibtex)
papers config git false       # stop committing (the backup directory stays)
papers config git-lfs true    # also back up the files (sets git true)

papers config git false also sets git-lfs to false. Libraries made by older papers versions keep their saved setting. The --no-git option of a command skips the commit of that command.

docs.title: What is backed up
docs.text:
Each save commits, in the backup directory:

  • a copy of the bibtex, under its own name (e.g. papers.bib);
  • the origin copies of the entries exchanged with a pool, .papers/origin/*.bib (one file per pool, see Pools);
  • .papers/distinct.json, the pairs recorded as not the same paper;
  • with git-lfs only: the attached files and backup_clean.bib (see git-lfs).

A command that changes no entry and no file of .papers/ (e.g. papers check that finds nothing, papers add of a duplicate that is skipped, a pull with nothing to take) does not write the bibtex and commits nothing.

The commit message is the command, e.g. papers add paper.pdf. A library file of .papers/ that was removed from the library is removed from the next snapshot. The library configuration, .papers/config.json, is not backed up: papers restore, undo and redo leave it as it is.

papers restore, undo and redo restore the bibtex and the files of .papers/ together. undo, redo and restore --ref COMMIT also remove the files of .papers/ that the restored snapshot does not have. Without the backup, papers undo only swaps the bibtex with its previous version (.papers.bib.backup, next to the bibtex), and papers restore is an error.

A commit that fails (e.g. refused by a git hook) prints a warning: the bibtex is saved anyway.

Each commit stores the whole bibtex; once the backup directory has 150 such objects (about 50 commits), the command that commits packs them with git repack, which keeps only the differences between versions (about 2 s for a library of 10000 entries, 9 s for 30000).

docs.title: Where
docs.text:
The backup directory is a subfolder of the backup folder of the machine, whatever the location of the library: ~/.local/share/papers/backups on Linux ($XDG_DATA_HOME/papers/backups when XDG_DATA_HOME is set), the platform's user data directory elsewhere (on macOS, ~/Library/Application Support/papers/backups). papers status -v shows the backup directory of the library:

* backup (git):       True
* backup files (git-lfs): False
* backup directory:   /home/me/.local/share/papers/backups/sealevel-papers-3f9a1c2b

The directory is named after the parent folder of the bibtex and the bibtex, plus a hash of the full path of the bibtex (e.g. sealevel-papers-3f9a1c2b for ~/projects/sealevel/papers.bib), so that two libraries never share a directory. The library configuration stores this name ("gitdir"), which each machine looks up in its own backup folder; a backup directory outside that folder is stored as an absolute path. Each backup directory also has a manifest.json (not committed) that records the bibtex it backs up.

papers backup list lists the backup directories papers knows of (those of the backup folder, those of ~/.local/share/papers/backups on other platforms than Linux, and the one of the current library), with the bibtex each backs up, whether that bibtex still exists, and the number of snapshots. papers backup remove NAME... removes backup directories, e.g. those whose library was deleted. NAME can be a glob pattern (papers backup remove 'old-*'). It asks before removing each directory, unless -y/--yes is passed (-f/--force is the deprecated form of -y). papers uninstall --remove-backup removes the backup directory of the library with its configuration.

docs.title: papers git
docs.text:
papers git ARGS... runs git ARGS... in the backup directory of the library, e.g.

papers git log --oneline
papers git remote add origin REMOTE-URL
papers git push -u origin main

The branch of the backup is main. When git fails, it prints its own error message, and papers exits with git's exit code. papers git needs a library whose backup directory exists.

The backup is separate from any git repository the library is in: papers never commits to the repository of a project, and papers git does not run in it. The backup history is still the basis of papers undo and papers redo in such a library. To commit only the configuration of a library to the repository of a project, see Configuration for the .gitignore lines.

docs.title: git-lfs
docs.text:
With git-lfs set, the attached files are also backed up. They are hard-linked into the files/ folder of the backup directory, which git-lfs tracks, and backup_clean.bib, a copy of the bibtex whose file links point into files/, is committed with them, so that the backup is self-contained. Background in issue 51.

  • Since the file in the backup directory is a hard link, a file edited in place in the library is also edited there, until the next save commits it. The git store of the backup (.git/lfs) keeps its own copy of each committed version of a file.
  • papers restore, undo and redo first reset the backup directory to the committed snapshot, so they restore the committed version of the files. A link of the restored bibtex to a file that no longer exists points to the copy in the backup directory, unless --restore-files is passed: then the file is copied back to where the bibtex links to it.

docs.title: Pools and shallow libraries
docs.text:
A pool is a library, with its own backup. A command that writes both a library and its pool (add in a shallow library, push, pull, sync, a command with auto-push) commits a snapshot in each backup, each with its own setting: the pool's commit is in the pool's backup directory. papers undo in the library undoes the change of the library only; papers -C POOL undo undoes the change of the pool (see Undo in a pool and Undo in a library that has a pool).

A shallow library links to the files of its pool. With git-lfs set in the shallow library, its backup hard-links and commits the pool files that its entries link to, the same way as the files of a self-contained library: a file shared with the pool is then in both backups if the pool also has git-lfs.

docs.title: Backups of earlier versions
docs.text:
• Backup directories created by older papers versions, named after the bibtex alone, keep their name and are used as they are. If a backup finds that its directory belongs to another library (its manifest.json names another bibtex), the library moves to a new backup directory instead of mixing the two histories, with an error message.
  • The libraries of papers 2.2 to 2.4 kept their backup in .papers/ next to the bibtex, the folder of config.json, origin/ and distinct.json since papers 3. The first backup moves that repository (its history and the files it tracks) to a new subfolder of the backup folder, with a warning, and the library configuration records it.
  • Backups made with git-lfs by earlier papers versions tracked files/, a pattern that git-lfs does not apply to the files in that folder (they were stored as plain git files). The next save adds files/** to .gitattributes and stores the files with git-lfs from then on.

docs.title: A global shared library
docs.text:
One way to use papers: a single library, for instance ~/Documents/papers, holds all your entries and PDFs, and each project is a shallow library that uses it as pool. A paper is fetched and stored once, the first time a project adds it; the other projects take it from the shared library. This is close to the global library of papers 2, with one bibtex per project on top.

papers supports this with an optional default library in the global configuration (~/.config/papers/config.json on Linux):

  • papers init --shallow creates a shallow library whose pool is the default library;
  • commands run outside of any library act on the default library.

docs.title: Create it
docs.text:
papers init PATH --global creates a self-contained library at PATH and registers it as the default library. PATH is required: papers init . --global registers the current directory.

$ papers init ~/Documents/papers --global
created the library ~/Documents/papers
* bibtex:  papers.bib
* files:   files (the files directory of the library)
* backup:  git
`papers status -v` shows all settings
registered ~/Documents/papers as the default library in ~/.config/papers/config.json

An existing library is registered with papers config --global default PATH. The default library must be a library without pool; papers config --global default none (or --unset default) removes the setting, and does not change the library.

$ papers config --global default
~/Documents/papers

docs.title: Projects that use it
docs.text:
$ cd ~/projects/ice
$ papers init --shallow
created the library ~/projects/ice
* bibtex:  papers.bib
* files:   in the pool (shallow library)
* pool:    ~/Documents/papers
* backup:  git
`papers status -v` shows all settings
$ papers add --doi 10.5194/esd-4-11-2013
Added -> perrette_landerer2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013) [also added to pool ~/Documents/papers]

papers init --shallow is papers init --pool ~/Documents/papers: the pool is written in the project's configuration as the global configuration writes it (with ~), so that a project copied to another machine with the same layout finds it there. Changing the default library later does not change the projects created before. Without a default library, papers init --shallow stops:

$ papers init --shallow
ERROR:papers:no default library: `papers init PATH --global` or `papers config --global default PATH`

See Shallow libraries for what a shallow library does with its pool: add looks in it first and adds the new papers to it, and papers sync exchanges the changes of the shared entries.

docs.title: Outside of any project
docs.text:
A command run outside of any library acts on the default library, and papers status says so:

$ cd ~
$ papers list
perrette_landerer2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013)
$ papers status
papers library: ~/Documents/papers (default library)
* files:              Documents/papers/files (the files directory of the library, empty)
* files mode:         move
* bibtex:             Documents/papers/papers.bib (1 entries, 0 file links)

The default library can take papers from other libraries too, e.g. a self-contained project (see Exchanges with any library):

$ papers add --pool ~/projects/sealevel --doi 10.5194/bg-8-515-2011
Added -> perrette_yool2011: Near-ubiquity of ice-edge blooms in the Arctic (doi:10.5194/bg-8-515-2011, file:1) [from pool ../../projects/sealevel]

Without a default library, a command outside of any library stops:

$ papers config --global default none
$ papers list
ERROR:papers:no library found here: `papers init`, or pass --bibtex
$ papers status
papers library: (no library found: create one with `papers init`)
* default library:    none

papers -C DIR runs a command in the library DIR from anywhere, e.g. papers -C ~/Documents/papers undo. papers uninstall run outside of any library does not remove the default library's configuration: run papers -C ~/Documents/papers uninstall for that.

docs.title: From papers 2
docs.text: The global library of papers 2 becomes the default library with papers migrate, where it is (see Upgrading from papers 2). Its project libraries become self-contained libraries; papers config pool PATH makes one of them a shallow library of the default library, once the default library has its PDFs (papers push --pool PATH --all copies them there).

docs.title: Install papers
docs.text:
papers 3 (beta) is published on PyPI as a pre-release: --pre installs it.

pip install --pre papers-cli

The development version, from the v3 branch:

pip install git+https://github.com/perrette/papers.git@v3

papers 2, the current release:

pip install papers-cli

Note there is another project registered on PyPI as papers, hence papers-cli for command-line-interface. The installed command is still papers. To upgrade a papers 2 setup, see Upgrading from papers 2.

docs.title: Name clash with GNOME Papers
docs.text:
The GNOME Papers document viewer (the default viewer on recent GNOME desktops) also installs a papers command; with both installed, whichever comes first in $PATH wins. Two mitigations are built in:

  • The package also installs the command under the unambiguous name papers-cli — call that, or set a shell alias (e.g. alias papers=papers-cli), on systems where the names collide.
  • Because this command may mask GNOME Papers, a call whose arguments are all existing files (paths or file:// URIs, as passed by file managers through the viewer's desktop entry) is handed over unchanged to the next papers executable in $PATH that is not this tool, i.e. GNOME Papers itself. Double-clicking a PDF and papers somefile.pdf therefore keep opening the viewer. If no other papers is found, the files are opened with the system's default viewer (xdg-open) instead; should that lead back to this command, it stops with an error rather than looping. Subcommand names always take precedence (papers ./list opens a file named list; papers list lists your library), and any flag disables the hand-over — call the viewer's binary directly for viewer-specific flags.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
• python 3.11+
  • PyMuPDF (preferred) or poppler-utils (only pdftotext and pdfinfo; deprecated): convert PDF to text for parsing
  • bibtexparser: parse bibtex files
  • scholarly: interface for google scholar
  • rapidfuzz: calculate score to sort crossref requests
  • unidecode: replace unicode with ascii equivalent

The Python dependencies are installed automatically with pip.

docs.title: Optional: RIS support
docs.text:
Reading and writing RIS files (papers add refs.ris, papers export --format ris, papers list --format ris) needs the rispy package, which is not installed by default. Install it in the environment of papers:

pip install 'papers-cli[ris]'       # with papers
pip install rispy                    # or afterwards
pipx inject papers-cli rispy         # papers installed with pipx
uv tool install papers-cli --with rispy   # papers installed with uv

When a command needs rispy and it is missing, papers asks in a terminal whether to install it with pip (python -m pip install rispy, with the Python of papers); otherwise, or on no, it stops without changing anything and prints these commands. CSL-JSON needs no extra package.

docs.title: Move library to a new location
docs.text:
Moving a library can be tricky. Simple cases are:

  • files are stored in a central repository, and the bibtex contains absolute paths. Then moving the bibtex by hand is fine.
  • files are stored alongside the bibtex, and the bibtex contains relative paths. Just move around the folder containing bibtex and files.

In any other cases, you risk breaking the file links.

Papers tries to be as little opinionated as possible about how files are organized, and so it relies on your own judgement and use case. When loading a bibtex, it always interprets relative file links as being relative to the bibtex file. When saving a bibtex, it will save file links according to the paths setting of the library (relative to the bibtex by default, see Configuration).

To move the files directory, or some of its files, use papers file mv: it updates the links of the entries, and the filesdir setting when the files directory itself moves (see Files):

papers file mv files ../shared/files

The following set of commands also works, provided the initial file links are valid (optional parameters in brackets):

touch new.bib
papers add /path/to/old.bib --bib new.bib [ --copy | --link ] [ --filesdir newfilesdir ]
rm -f /path/to/old.bib

By default the files of old.bib are moved into the files directory (--copy keeps them in place too, --link links to them where they are), except the files inside the files directory of another library, which are copied.

docs.title: Duplicates
docs.text:
It's easy to end up with duplicates in your bibtex. After adding PDFs, or every once in a while, do:

papers check --duplicates

It groups the entries that are the same paper, by the rule of papers add (same DOI, arXiv id, ISBN of two books, or else same authors and title; see Adding entries), and merges each group into one entry. A group never holds two entries with different DOIs: a copy without DOI that matches both goes with one of them, and the other comes up on the next check if it is still a match.

Entry 1 of a group, the target, is the entry with most fields. The merge works as in papers add: the target keeps its key, fields missing in it are added, the file links are kept. The other entries are removed, and their keys are added to the biblatex ids field of the target, so that \cite commands with the old keys keep working with biblatex (BibTeX ignores the field). Commands that take a KEY also accept a key of the ids field.

$> papers check --duplicates
Same paper: 2 entries (same title and authors)
  1  smith2020climate  article  doi 10.1000/abc123  files/smith.pdf
  2  Smith_2020        article  no doi              other/smith-preprint.pdf

@article{smith2020climate,
!  key      = smith2020climate
!             2: Smith_2020 (kept in ids)
   author   = {Smith, John and Doe, Jane}
   doi      = {10.1000/abc123}
+  file     = {files/smith.pdf;other/smith-preprint.pdf}
+  ids      = {Smith_2020}
!  journal  = {Nature}
!             2: {Nature Climate Change}
   keywords = {climate, mine}
   title    = {Climate sensitivity revisited}
   year     = {2020}
}
1 conflict. Entry 2 is removed after the merge; its key goes to ids.
  1 keep values of 1   2 take values of 2   f field by field   e edit
  t N make entry N the target   n not the same paper   s skip   q quit   ? help
>>> 1
merged into smith2020climate: Smith_2020 (kept in ids)

The answers are those of the dialogue of papers add (see Adding entries), with one more: t N makes entry N the target, so that its key is kept. n (not the same paper) leaves the entries as they are and records them in .papers/distinct.json, so that the next check does not ask again. A group whose entries differ only by key and file links is merged without a question.

--on-duplicate sets what to do with each group without asking:

Value What happens ask the dialogue (default when the standard input is a terminal) keep merge; conflicts keep the value of entry 1 skip leave the groups as they are (the default with -y/--yes) error exit with status 1 if there is any group, and list them (default without a terminal)

Groups that the title guard asks about (same DOI, but different entry types and titles) are never merged with keep.

To only see the groups, use papers list --duplicates (see Listing).

The -m/--mode option of earlier versions still works, with a warning: -m i is --on-duplicate ask, -m m is keep, -m s is skip. To remove entries, use papers rm.

docs.title: Checking and fixing files
docs.text:
papers file check reports broken links, files linked twice, identical files and, with --metadata, DOIs of PDFs that differ from their entry's DOI. It changes nothing. papers file fix applies the safe repairs only. Broken links are removed with papers file detach --broken:

papers file check
papers file fix
papers file detach --broken

papers file rename places the files in the files directory under their template name (see Renaming files and keys).

papers file clean removes the files of the files directory (and its subfolders) that no entry links to:

papers file clean

It asks before removing anything, unless -y/--yes is passed. It ignores hidden files and folders and .bib files; a folder with a .{folder}.bib file inside, which is how versions before 2.19 stored entries with several files (see Renaming files and keys), is removed as a whole when no entry links to its files. That command works best when the files are in their own folder, and not mixed up with other things, obviously.

papers file clean --dry-run --yes lists the files that no entry links to, without removing them: a way to check what is actually tracked and what is not.

See Files for all the papers file commands. papers filecheck is the deprecated form of these commands (it still works, with a warning).

docs.title: Listing and searching
docs.text: papers list is a powerful command, inspired by unix's find and grep. It lets you search your bibtex, output the result in a number of formats, or perform actions on the matched entries.

docs.title: Basic listing
docs.text:
Pretty listing by default (otherwise pass --plain for plain bibtex):

$> papers list
Perrette2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1)

docs.title: Search with keywords
docs.text:
Search with any number of keywords:

$> papers list perrette scaling approach sea level
... (short list)
$> papers list perrette scaling approach sea level --any
... (long list)
$> papers list --key perrette2013 --author perrette --year 2013 --title scaling approach sea level
... (precise list)

With --invert, papers list lists the entries that the same command without --invert does not list.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Tags are the keywords field of the entries (comma-separated). papers tag lists them with the number of entries, adds and removes them:

$> papers tag perrette2013 --add sea-level projections
$> papers tag
sea-level (12)
projections (3)
$> papers tag perrette2013 --rm projections
$> papers tag --rename sea-level sea-level-rise     # in the whole library
$> papers list --tag sea-level projections
Perrette2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1, sea-level | projections )

papers list ... --add-tag TAG... adds tags to the listed entries.

docs.title: Output formats
docs.text:
papers list supports a number of special flags such as --duplicates, --review-required, --broken-file. --format chooses the output:

  • --format line (the default): one line per entry (also -l, -1, --one-liner);
  • --format bibtex: the entries as bibtex (also --plain);
  • --format ris, --format csl-json: the entries as RIS or CSL-JSON, with the file links as absolute paths (RIS needs the rispy package; see Export for the conversion);
  • --format key: the keys only, one per line (also -K, --key-only), to pipe into other commands (below).

--field FIELD... prints the key and the given fields of each entry (--no-key leaves the key out). -f is a deprecated alias of --field: in v4, -f is no longer --field (it means --force in other commands).

docs.title: Duplicates
docs.text:
papers list --duplicates lists the entries that are the same paper, by the rule of papers add (see Adding entries): the groups that papers check --duplicates would merge or ask about, and not the pairs recorded as distinct in .papers/distinct.json. With --invert, it lists the other entries.

With --fuzzy, it also lists the entries whose authors and title are similar (rapidfuzz token set ratio of at least --fuzzy-ratio, default 80). This is for looking only: papers never merges entries on this score.

With --by key, --by doi or --by title, it lists instead the entries that share that field: the same key (ignoring case), the same DOI, or the same title (ignoring case and punctuation), whether or not they are the same paper by the rule above (--by implies --duplicates).

--duplicates-key, --duplicates-doi and --duplicates-tit are deprecated forms of --duplicates --by key, --by doi and --by title; --similarity is deprecated and has no effect.

docs.title: Naming entries
docs.text:
The commands that act on entries take KEY arguments, where KEY is any of:

  • the key of the entry (case-insensitive), or a former key listed in its biblatex ids field (comma-separated); the key of an entry names that entry even if it is also a former key of another entry;
  • a DOI: 10.1000/xyz, also written doi:10.1000/xyz or https://doi.org/10.1000/xyz (case-insensitive);
  • an arXiv identifier: 2101.01234, 2101.01234v2, arXiv:2101.01234, or of the old style hep-th/9901001; it matches the eprint field (when archivePrefix is arXiv or absent) and arXiv DOIs (10.48550/arXiv.<id>), whatever the version;
  • an ISBN, 10 or 13 digits, with hyphens or spaces (the ISBN-10 and ISBN-13 forms of a book are the same), matched against the isbn field.

A key cannot start with a digit, so an argument that starts with a digit is never a key. An identifier that matches no entry, or several entries (e.g. an ISBN shared by the chapters of a book), is an error, reported before anything changes.

docs.title: Piping
docs.text:
- reads the identifiers from the standard input, one per line (blank lines are ignored). papers list -K prints the keys of the listed entries, one per line:

papers list smith 2020 -K | papers file rename -
papers list --tag to-read -K | papers open -
papers list --no-file -K | papers check --fetch -
papers list --review-required -K | papers edit -

These commands take -: edit, rm, tag, open, check, and the papers file commands that act on entries (rename, check, and the --key option of detach and rm).

docs.title: Actions on the listed entries
docs.text:
papers list can run a command on the entries it lists: list the entries, then act on them. Each action calls the same code as the command it stands for, with the listed entries as KEY...:

action command example -e/--edit papers edit KEY... papers list --duplicates --edit --delete (--delete-files, --keep-files) papers rm KEY... (same options) papers list --tag draft --delete --keep-files --add-tag TAG... papers tag --add TAG... KEY... papers list -a perrette --add-tag ocean --rm-tag TAG... papers tag --rm TAG... KEY... papers list --tag to-read --rm-tag to-read --rename (--keep-source) papers file rename KEY... (--keep-source) papers list smith 2020 --rename --attach FILE... papers file attach KEY FILE... papers list --title "ice-edge blooms" --attach si.pdf --detach [FILE...] papers file detach [FILE...] --key KEY... papers list --year 2010 --detach --detach-broken papers file detach --broken --key KEY... papers list --broken-file --detach-broken --fix-files [DIR...] (--pool PATH, --move) papers file fix KEY... [--search DIR...] (--pool PATH, --move) papers list --broken-file --fix-files ~/pdfs -o/--open papers open KEY... papers list --tag to-read --open --push (--pool PATH, --on-duplicate) papers push KEY... (same options) papers list --tag thesis --push --pull (--pool PATH, --on-duplicate) papers pull KEY... (same options) papers list --tag thesis --pull --sync (--pool PATH, --on-duplicate) papers sync KEY... (same options) papers list --tag thesis --sync --export DIR (--export-format, --export-files) papers export DIR KEY... (--format, --files) papers list -a perrette --export out --export-format ris

Notes on the options:

  • --delete asks, in a terminal, whether to delete the files of the entries too; --delete-files and --keep-files answer without asking (see Files).
  • --attach needs exactly one listed entry: with none or several, it is an error and nothing changes. The files are moved, copied or linked as the files setting says.
  • --detach without FILE removes all the links of the listed entries.
  • The folders given to --fix-files are the --search folders of papers file fix: the broken links are also looked for there. --move moves the files found there instead of copying them.
  • --pool PATH is the library to exchange with for --push, --pull and --sync (once), and a library to look for files in for --fix-files (can be repeated).
  • --export-format and --export-files are the --format and --files options of papers export (--format of papers list is the format of its own output).
  • --detach and --fix-files take any number of values: write them after the search words, or end their values with another option.
  • An option of an action without the action (e.g. --move without --fix-files) is an error.

The action runs in the same process as the listing: papers can ask questions and open the editor, and the library is saved once (one backup snapshot, undone by one papers undo). One action at a time: two actions in the same command are an error, and nothing changes.

(papers check --duplicates merges duplicates, see Managing your library.) The other commands that act on entries, e.g. papers check, read the keys of papers list -K with - (see Piping).

These forms are deprecated, print a warning that shows the new form, and will be removed in v4:

Deprecated New form papers list ... --copy papers list ... --rename --keep-source papers list ... --add-files FILE... papers list ... --attach FILE... papers list ... --fetch papers list ... -K \| papers check --fetch --fetch-all --fix-doi --fix-key --format-name -

--add-files keeps its papers 2 behaviour: it links the files where they are, or moves them with --rename, or copies them with --copy. --attach follows the files setting.

docs.title: Libraries and pools
docs.text:
A library is a bibtex file, a files directory and a configuration file (.papers/config.json), as created by papers init (see Configuration). Each project usually has its own library.

A pool is a library that another library takes entries from or exchanges entries with. Nothing in a library marks it as a pool: any library without pool of its own can serve as one, and a pool can be used by several libraries.

A library is in one of two states, given by its pool setting alone:

  • self-contained: no pool (pool: none, or no pool setting). The library has its own entries and its own PDFs, in its files directory. papers init creates such a library.
  • shallow: a pool, the path of another library. The library takes its entries from the pool and links to the pool's PDFs. papers init --pool PATH creates such a library. See Shallow libraries.

Any library, self-contained or shallow, can also exchange entries with another library given on the command line, --pool PATH, e.g. a folder shared with a coauthor (see Exchanges with any library).

What a library does with its pool, or with the library of --pool PATH:

  • papers add looks in the pool first (papers add --pool PATH looks in PATH);
  • papers pull updates the entries shared with the pool, and adds the entries of the pool named, or all of them with --all;
  • papers push updates the entries shared with the pool, and adds the entries named, or all of them with --all;
  • papers sync does both;
  • papers status (pool of a shallow library) and papers pull --check tell whether the pool changed since the last exchange with it: up to date, or changed since last pull or push;
  • papers file fix relinks the broken links to the files of the pool entry of the same paper (papers file fix --pool PATH also looks in PATH, which may have a pool itself; nothing changes in PATH and no origin copy is recorded, see Reconnecting PDFs and a bibtex).

An entry is shared with a pool when the pool has the same paper: the pool entry of its origin copy (see Origin copies), else the same paper by the same-paper rule (see Keys and identity). Without KEY or --all, pull, push and sync exchange the shared entries only, with an origin copy or not.

An exchange goes one level only: the pool has no pool, and a library given with --pool PATH must have none either (PATH has a pool itself).

Nothing is pulled automatically. Nothing is pushed automatically, except in a shallow library: add adds the new entries to the pool, the file links of an entry are updated in the pool entry, and with the auto-push setting the changes of the shared entries are pushed too (see Shallow libraries). An older project does not change because of work in a newer one.

The Quickstart shows a self-contained project and a shallow project that uses it. A global shared library describes one library used as the pool of all projects.

docs.title: Merging
docs.text:
pull, push and sync merge each entry field by field. The origin copy is papers' memory of the entry at the last exchange (see Origin copies). Comparing each side with it tells which side changed a field. A removed field counts as a change:

Field since the origin copy Result changed or removed on the side that sends only (the pool for pull, the library for push) taken changed or removed on the side that receives only (e.g. a field adapted to a journal style) kept, without asking changed on both sides to different values, or removed on one side and changed on the other a conflict removed on both sides removed

Conflicts are decided in the dialogue or with --on-duplicate (see papers pull and papers push). An entry without origin copy has no base: each field that differs is a conflict. The first exchange of such an entry (e.g. the first sync with a library given with --pool PATH that has papers of the library) asks about these conflicts once: afterwards the origin copy is recorded, and the next exchanges merge three-way.

docs.title: Removed entries
docs.text:
An entry is never removed by an exchange:

  • papers rm KEY removes the entry from the library only. push and sync do not remove it from the pool.
  • An entry removed from the pool stays in the libraries that have it. It is no longer shared: pull, push and sync without KEY or --all (and the auto-push of a shallow library) leave it out, and note it once:
smith2020: removed from pool ~/Documents/papers (`papers push smith2020` adds it back)

Its origin copy for the pool is dropped, so the note does not come again. push KEY and push --all add it to the pool again; pull KEY reports it as Not found; pull --check lists it with the note (and drops nothing). Remove it from the library with papers rm KEY.

docs.title: papers pull
docs.text:
papers pull [KEY...|-] [--all] [--pool PATH] [--on-duplicate MODE] [--check]

Without KEY, pull updates the entries shared with the pool (the pool has the same paper). For each of them (or each entry named, or every entry with --all), papers finds its entry in the pool (by its origin copy, else by the same-paper rule) and merges it into the library entry, field by field (see Merging). The pool is the side that sends: a field changed or removed in the pool only is taken (+ in the dialogue, (removed) for a removal), a field changed in the library only is kept, and a conflict is marked !.

File links are merged: new files of the pool entry are linked in a shallow library (from its own pool), and otherwise copied into the files directory as the files setting says. The key of the library entry never changes. After the merge, the origin copy is the pool's current version. A skipped conflict leaves the pool shown as changed in papers status.

An entry without origin copy (added before the pool was used, or with --no-pool) is matched to the pool by the same-paper rule. Its differences with the pool entry are conflicts (there is no origin to tell which side changed), a field that only the pool entry has is added, and the origin copy is recorded afterwards ("linked").

An entry that the pool does not have is reported (Not found) only when it is named on the command line. Without KEY, it is left as it is (with a note if it was removed from the pool, see Removed entries).

A KEY is looked up in the library first, then in the pool (its key, DOI, arXiv identifier or ISBN): an entry of the pool that the library does not have is added to it (added), with its origin copy, under the pool key (see Keys and identity); its files are linked in a shallow library, otherwise copied as the files setting says (a hard link when possible). An identifier found in neither is an error, and nothing is changed. --all adds every entry of the pool that the library does not have (same-paper rule). A pool that does not exist or is not a library is an error of pull, pull --check and sync, and nothing is changed (papers init PATH creates it). Without --pool PATH, a self-contained library has no pool to pull from: this library has no pool: give one with --pool PATH.

pull prints one line per entry added (Added ->), modified (Modified ->), left with a conflict (Conflict ->) or, among the entries named, not found in the pool (Not found ->), with the pool in brackets, then the counts when more than one entry changed or was not exchanged: added, modified, skipped, not found, and linked (an entry without origin copy, the same as its pool entry: its origin copy is recorded). The entries unchanged are not counted. When nothing changed, pull prints one line, nothing to pull from pool ../sealevel. push prints the same lines for the pool entries. When a command also adds or changes the entry in the pool (see Auto-push), or add takes it from the pool, its line says so in brackets: [also added to pool ~/Documents/papers], [also modified in pool ~/Documents/papers], [not pushed: changed in the pool too; papers sync decides], [from pool ~/Documents/papers].

Conflicts are decided as for duplicates (see The dialogue), with --on-duplicate:

Mode Conflicts ask (default in a terminal) the dialogue: 1 keeps the library values, 2 takes the pool values, f goes field by field (also through the changes from the pool), e edits, s skips, q quits keep the library values are kept update the pool values are taken skip the entry is not changed, and its origin copy is not updated: it comes again next time error (default without a terminal) stop before saving anything

Fields changed in the pool only need no decision: they are taken in every mode.

papers pull --check only reports: whether the pool changed since the last pull (a modification time check), and the entries whose pool version changed since their origin copy, with the fields (without KEY, the entries shared with the pool). papers status shows the first part too, for the pool of a shallow library.

docs.title: papers push
docs.text:
papers push [KEY...|-] [--all] [--pool PATH] [--on-duplicate MODE]

The reverse of pull, into the pool of the library or the library of --pool PATH. Without KEY, only the entries shared with the pool (the pool has the same paper) are pushed; an entry removed from the pool is not added back (see Removed entries). push KEY... pushes the entries named, and push --all every entry of the library:

  • an entry that is not in the pool is added to it, with a key from the pool's key template; its files are copied into the pool's files directory (a hard link when possible), named with the pool's name template;
  • an entry that is in the pool is merged three-way into the pool entry: fields changed or removed in the library only are taken, fields changed or removed in the pool only are kept, conflicts are decided with --on-duplicate (keep: the pool values, update: the library values). The pool key does not change.

Push does not change the library: after it, the origin copy is the library version that was pushed, and the fields that only the pool entry has come with the next pull (or papers sync). A pool that does not exist or is not a library is an error of push, and nothing is changed: the message suggests papers init PATH (and, when the parent folder of PATH is missing too, that a disk may not be mounted).

docs.title: papers sync
docs.text:
papers sync [KEY...|-] [--all] [--pool PATH] [--on-duplicate MODE]

runs papers pull, then papers push of the same entries:

  • without KEY, the entries shared with the pool (the pool has the same paper). An entry that the pool does not have is not exchanged: name it, or use --all;
  • with KEY..., the entries named. A KEY that only the pool has is added to the library, as with pull, and a KEY that only the library has is added to the pool, as with push;
  • with --all, pull --all then push --all: each side gets the entries it does not have.

If the pull leaves conflicts undecided (skipped, or the dialogue quit), nothing is pushed: decide them with papers pull, then sync again. When nothing changed, sync prints one line:

$ papers sync
nothing to sync with pool ../sealevel

docs.title: Keys and identity
docs.text:
The key of an entry belongs to each library: it is what LaTeX documents cite. pull and push never change the key of an entry that the library they write to has. An entry new to the pool gets a key from the pool's key template; an entry of the pool new to the library keeps the pool key, with a letter suffix if the library has that key already (Smith_2020b).

Three fields are not merged by pull and push: each side keeps its own.

  • the key, as above;
  • ids, the former keys of the entry in that library: they mean nothing in the other library;
  • file, the links of each library to its own copies of the files. A file that the other side has and this side does not is linked or copied (see papers pull and papers push).

A library entry and a pool entry are matched by the same rule as duplicates (see Same paper): same DOI, arXiv identifier, ISBN (two books), or else the same authors and title. The pairs recorded as "not the same paper" (.papers/distinct.json) are merged both ways on pull and push.

An entry with an origin copy is first looked up under the pool key of its origin copy: that pool entry is taken if it is the same paper as the origin copy or as the entry. Otherwise, e.g. when the pool key now names another paper, the pool entry is found by the rule above (from the origin copy, then from the entry), and last under the pool key, if its DOI, arXiv identifier and ISBN do not differ from those of the origin copy (both titles changed). When the pool has the same paper twice, the entry of the origin copy is the one exchanged.

docs.title: Origin copies
docs.text:
.papers/origin/, next to the bibtex of the library, holds one file per pool: the pool of the library, and each library exchanged with through --pool PATH. A file is named after the folder of the pool and the start of a hash of its path as the library names it, e.g. shared-with-bob-d15650.bib for ../shared-with-bob, or papers-<hash>.bib for ~/Documents/papers. The first lines of the file name the pool and give the modification time of its bibtex at the last exchange. In a library whose pool is ../shared-with-bob, after papers pull agnew_farrell1978 and papers pull:

@comment{papers-pool ../shared-with-bob}

@comment{papers-pulled 1792681264781917448}

@article{agnew_farrell1978,
 author = {Agnew, D. C. and Farrell, W. E.},
 papers-pool-key = {agnew_farrell1978},
 papers-time = {2026-10-22T17:01:45+02:00},
 title = {Self-consistent equilibrium ocean tides},
 year = {1978}
}

The file records, for each entry exchanged with the pool (by add, pull or push), its origin copy, under the library's key, with the key in the pool (papers-pool-key) and the time (papers-time). In a shallow library, the origin copy for its pool also keeps its file field, the file links of the pool entry after the exchange, so that a pull can tell a link that the pool entry removed from one it never had (the origin copies for other libraries have no file field). The file links are not part of the three-way merge. The modification time is recorded at a pull of all entries that skipped no conflict, or a push or an add when the pool had not changed since the previous exchange (or when it is the first exchange). A push that leaves the pool entry with fields or files that the library entry does not have does not count: papers status then shows the pool as changed until the next pull. The files are part of the git backup of the library (see Git integration).

The files of all pools are kept: after papers config pool PATH, the library uses the file of PATH (with the origin copies of the exchanges with --pool PATH, if any), and setting the pool back to an earlier one finds its origin copies again.

Earlier v3 beta versions kept all the origin copies in one file, .papers/origin.bib: papers splits it into these files the first time it reads it, and removes it.

The origin copy is the third version of a three-way merge. It is the version of the side that sent the entry, as it was sent: the pool entry after add and pull, the library entry after push. What the receiving side has beyond it is a change of that side, for the next exchange the other way: a field that only the pool entry has comes with the next pull; a field that only the library entry has goes to the pool with the next push.

papers add other.bib copies the entries of other.bib once, and keeps no memory of where they came from. The entries taken with papers pull stay linked to the pool through their origin copy: later pulls bring the corrections made in the pool.

docs.title: Exchanges with any library
docs.text:
--pool PATH on pull, push and sync exchanges with the library at PATH, from any library: self-contained or shallow. PATH must be a library without pool: no command creates it, papers init PATH does. The exchange works as with the pool of a library:

  • the origin copies are recorded for PATH, in its own file of .papers/origin/: the next exchange with PATH is a three-way merge, and a field changed on one side only needs no decision;
  • without KEY or --all, the exchange handles the entries shared with PATH (PATH has the same paper);
  • papers sync --pool PATH KEY... takes the entries named from PATH that the library does not have, sends to PATH those that it does not have, and merges the others both ways;
  • papers pull --pool PATH --all takes every entry of PATH, and papers push --pool PATH --all sends every entry of the library.

An entry that has no origin copy for PATH yet (the first exchange) has no base: each field that differs is a conflict, decided in the dialogue or with --on-duplicate.

$ papers sync --pool ../shared-with-bob
nothing to sync with pool ../shared-with-bob: no entries shared with it (`papers sync --pool ../shared-with-bob --all` adds the entries missing on each side)

The files are copied, as the files setting says (a file of PATH is never moved): the entries taken from PATH get copies of its files (a hard link when possible) and the entries sent to PATH get copies of theirs in its files directory. The file links of a shallow library are those of the pool entries for its own pool only. A shallow library that takes entries from PATH places their files in the files directory of its pool, and adds the entries new to the library to its pool, as add does (also added to pool ...); the changes of the fields go to the pool with papers push, or with auto-push. See Topic libraries for an example.

papers config pool PATH makes PATH the pool of the library (see Changing the pool); the origin copies recorded for PATH stay valid, however PATH is written.

A folder shared with a coauthor, exchanged with from time to time:

cd ~/projects/sealevel
papers export ../shared-with-bob mine2022 smith2020   # a self-contained library for Bob
papers sync --pool ../shared-with-bob                  # the changes of the shared entries, both ways
papers sync --pool ../shared-with-bob --all            # also the entries missing on each side

papers export is described in Export.

docs.title: add looks in the pool first
docs.text:
When the paper added is already in the pool, papers add takes the pool's entry, without querying crossref:

  • a PDF with the same content as a file of a pool entry, or whose DOI (from the PDF metadata, or a DOI of its text whose title in the pool appears in the text) is in the pool;
  • a DOI (papers add --doi DOI) that a pool entry has;
  • a key (papers add --key KEY, with no file, DOI or other field) that a pool entry has, ignoring case: the entry keeps the pool key. Without such an entry (and without a library entry of that key), add stops with an error;
  • an entry of an added bibtex that is the same paper as a pool entry: the pool's fields are taken, the entry keeps its key, and its fields that the pool entry does not have are kept.

The entry gets the pool's files: in a shallow library, the entry links to the pool's file; otherwise, in copy and move mode they are copied into the library's files directory (a hard link when possible), named with the library's name template, and in link mode the entry links to the pool's file. A pool file is never moved. A PDF given that has the same content as a file of the pool entry is removed in move mode, since it is stored already, and kept in copy and link mode; a PDF with other content is attached to the entry as another file, placed as the files mode says. The origin copy is recorded. --no-pool skips the lookup.

docs.title: add --pool PATH
docs.text: papers add --pool PATH looks in the library PATH instead (PATH must be a library without pool), in the same way: a paper that PATH has is taken from it with its files, copied as the files mode says (in a shallow library, into the files directory of its pool, and the entry goes to its pool too, as any new entry), and the origin copy is recorded for PATH, so that papers pull --pool PATH brings the later corrections. Nothing new is sent to PATH. This is not papers -C PATH add, which adds to the library PATH.

docs.title: A pool with entries papers cannot read
docs.text: An entry that the bibtex parser cannot read, such as one with a field given twice or a missing brace, is kept in the file as it is, but papers does not see it. Every command that loads that bibtex warns about it, with its line. Papers does not write to a pool that has such an entry: it would not find that paper there, and would add it again. push, sync and the commands that add to the pool stop with an error, and nothing is changed, until the entry is fixed in the pool's bibtex. Reading from the pool (pull, add looking in the pool) still works.

docs.title: A finished paper
docs.text: Do not sync the library of a finished paper. Its keys stay as they are, but a pull can change journal abbreviations and other fields that the paper was written with. Leave auto-push off there, and do not pull.

docs.title: Undo in a pool
docs.text: A pool is a library with its own backup history (see Git integration). papers undo in a library undoes a change of that library only: an entry that add also added to the pool stays in the pool. To undo a change in the pool, run the command in the pool, e.g. papers -C ../sealevel undo. The origin copies of the library are restored with its bibtex: see Undo in a library that has a pool.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
papers works like git: one command with subcommands, run inside a project folder that holds a library. A library is a bibtex file, a configuration file (.papers/config.json) and, if it keeps its own PDFs, a files/ folder.

This page shows two cases: a self-contained project, with its own bibtex and PDFs, and a shallow project that uses the first one as its pool.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The 3.0 beta is published on PyPI as a pre-release:

pip install --pre papers-cli

See Installation for the requirements.

docs.title: 1. A self-contained project
docs.text:
papers init creates a self-contained library: its own entries, and its own PDFs in files/.

$ cd ~/projects/sealevel
$ papers init
created the library ~/projects/sealevel
* bibtex:  papers.bib
* files:   files (the files directory of the library)
* backup:  git
`papers status -v` shows all settings
$ papers add ~/Downloads/esd-4-11-2013.pdf
Added -> perrette_landerer2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1)
$ papers add --doi 10.1111/j.1365-246X.1978.tb04232.x
Added -> bretreger_mather1978: Modelling ocean-loading effects on tidal gravity in Australi... (doi:10.1111/j.1365-246X.1978.tb04232.x)

The DOI is read from the PDF, the entry is fetched from crossref, and the PDF is moved to files/ and renamed after the entry.

A self-contained library is also a library that other projects can use.

docs.title: 2. A shallow project that uses it
docs.text:
papers init --pool PATH creates a shallow library: it takes its entries from the library PATH, its pool, and links to the PDFs there. PATH is a self-contained library, such as the project above, or a library kept for sharing, e.g. ~/Documents/papers (see A global shared library).

$ cd ~/projects/tides
$ papers init --pool ../sealevel
created the library ~/projects/tides
* bibtex:  papers.bib
* files:   in the pool (shallow library)
* pool:    ../sealevel
* backup:  git
`papers status -v` shows all settings
$ papers add --doi 10.5194/esd-4-11-2013
Added -> perrette_landerer2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1) [from pool ../sealevel]
$ papers add ~/Downloads/bg-8-515-2011.pdf
Added -> perrette_yool2011: Near-ubiquity of ice-edge blooms in the Arctic (doi:10.5194/bg-8-515-2011, file:1) [also added to pool ../sealevel]

add looks in the pool first: a paper the pool has is taken from it, with its PDF, and nothing is fetched or copied. A new paper goes to the library and to the pool, and its PDF to the pool's files/. Each library has only the entries it asks for: tides has two entries, sealevel three.

Changes to the shared entries, made in either project, are exchanged with papers sync. After a tag added in sealevel:

$ papers sync
Modified -> perrette_landerer2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1, sea-level) [from pool ../sealevel]

docs.text:
